item.title: Post Malone Previews “Bad Mood”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Post Malone previewed "Bad Mood" as the wait for Eternal Buzz continued, following his latest comments about a huge album.
item.content:encoded:
Post Malone shared another taste of The Eternal Buzz on October 28, previewing a song apparently called “Bad Mood” while the album wait continued.

According to Billboard, the Instagram clip showed him listening on a couch with a beer. His #badmood hashtag suggested the title, while his caption again teased the album as coming soon. Billboard heard echoes of his beerbongs & bentleys era in the new snippet.

The preview followed another big claim about the size of the project. During his performance at the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix, Post told the crowd the record had around 50 songs, according to Holler. That number was larger than the two sets of 20 tracks shown when he first teased the project in April.

Questions about his next sound were already part of the conversation this summer. AllHipHop covered a separate July preview that had listeners talking about his return to rap after his country pivot. That clip included a reference to Stoney, his 2016 album. The possibility of a record divided between country and rap remained a theory in that report, which tied the renewed interest to the melodic sound of Stoney and beerbongs & bentleys.

His catalog gives both groups of listeners a reason to pay attention. Twelve Carat Toothache included appearances from Roddy Ricch, Doja Cat and Gunna. On F-1 Trillion, Post worked with Morgan Wallen, Tim McGraw and Dolly Parton. The latter record also paired him with Jelly Roll on “Losers” and Luke Combs on “Guy For That.” Those albums show the range behind the genre question surrounding his next project, from rap guests to established country stars.

The Grand Prix update offered another sign of how large he was thinking, though a rough count from the stage was not a final tracklist. The earlier April image pointed toward 40 songs across two discs. His latest estimate put the total closer to 50. At the same performance, he thanked fans for their support over the years and told them the new music was on its way. He also warned the crowd to “Listen in moderation” when the record arrived.

item.title: Too $hort Explains How Cash Demand From The Pack’s Friends Led To Signing
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Too $hort recalled The Pack's friends seeking money for an introduction before he signed the group behind the 2006 hit "Vans".
item.content:encoded:
Too $hort said The Pack’s friends demanded money for an introduction without the group knowing.

In his new Pitchfork interview, he recalled hearing their mixtape and meeting the friends at a hamburger stand. After calls revealed one member was his friend’s son, he reached out and signed them.

“We sitting in front of a hamburger stand and they like, ‘We ain’t the Pack, but the Pack is our homies, but you can’t get to the Pack unless you go through us ‘… they was just talking about how much money they gonna be getting from me. That was so unprofessional. I did my due diligence and called around and found out one of the dudes in the Pack was my homeboy’s son…That was their homies; they intercepted the call to try to get something out of it. The Pack didn’t even know,” Too $hort revealed.

The deal worked out well. According to $hort, he took them on the road, and the group was popular everywhere they went. The group also introduced him to MySpace.

His interest in the group fit a wider push for young Bay Area acts. In a 2006 San Francisco Chronicle interview, he said he wanted hyphy to create jobs and major-label deals.

He helped The Pack reach Jive while leaving their music in their hands. He said he didn’t make their beats or choose their song titles. His role was to spot talent and give it a shot.

That support also showed up on his own label’s releases. The Pack joined the lineup of I Love The Bay, a compilation released July 17, 2007. It put the group on a project with E-40, Keak Da Sneak, Messy Marv, Yukmouth and San Quinn, among others.

The album also included Zion I, The Team and a posthumous appearance by Mac Dre. Its track list paired The Pack with Mistah FAB on “Yes Sir.” The first singles were “Lose It,” featuring Mistah FAB and “Video Vixen,” featuring Dem Hoodstarz.

“I always wanted to represent the entire Bay Area,” Short said in AllHipHop’s coverage of the compilation. The release gave that aim a concrete form, with younger acts and established names sharing the same album.

The Pack’s own business moved on from Short’s label.

As AllHipHop reported in 2010, the Berkeley group included Lil Uno, Stunnaman, Lil B and producer Young L. They had been signed to his Up All Nite imprint, with distribution through Jive Records.

Their 2006 single “Vans” had sold more than 300,000 copies by May 19, 2010, when SMC Recordings announced a deal with them. The plan called for an album titled Wolfpack Party, with The Cataracs among its guests.

SMC’s interest had started before that deal. Will Bronson, then the company’s chief operating officer, said he tried to sign The Pack when “Vans” broke, but competing with Too $hort got in the way.

Too $hort told Pitchfork that he is still cool with the group and that he brings them out on stage to perform “Vans” to this day.

item.title: Megan Thee Stallion Puts Tina Snow In Diamonds
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Megan Thee Stallion showed off a Tina Snow chain by Elliott Eliantte, turning her rap alter ego into a custom diamond piece.
item.content:encoded:
Megan Thee Stallion gave Tina Snow her own diamonds, showing off a custom chain that turned her rap alter ego into jewelry.

The rapper shared the piece Tuesday, October 27. According to TAG24, Elliott Eliantte made the chain, which paired the letter T with a snowflake.

“I tell him exactly what I want and my boy brings it to life,” Megan wrote in the caption quoted by the outlet.

Tina has a history that reaches well beyond a new necklace. The name came from Pimp C’s Tony Snow persona, a tribute to a rapper Megan counted among her biggest influences. Her 2018 interview with The FADER placed that connection in her hometown of Houston, where she spoke about keeping a home even as her career grew.

That early interview also explained the voice behind Tina. Megan listened to Pimp C, the Notorious B.I.G. and Three 6 Mafia and wanted women to have room to be as blunt about sex as men were. Her songs let women take the lead, with the same self-belief that male rappers brought to their records.

“I really feel like if men can talk this much shit, women can too,” she told The FADER.

The persona gave her space to play with different sides of herself. In that interview, she described changing as part of growing rather than staying locked into one character. The new pendant used the name she had already built through that music.

Her Tina Snow EP arrived June 8, 2018, according to Apple Music’s catalog. The 10-song project ran 30 minutes, giving the character a full release years before the custom piece.

Megan’s say in the design also fit the control she had sought in her music business. As AllHipHop previously reported, her August distribution partnership with Interscope left her independent, with ownership of her masters and control over her creative work.

Roc Nation joined her in that partnership. The arrangement gave Megan major-label distribution while letting her keep the rights and creative freedom at the center of the deal. It followed a 2024 distribution agreement with Warner Music Group that had also preserved her independence.

item.title: J. Cole Rejects Retirement – “I’m Not Using That Word”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: J. Cole rejected the retirement label in a new GQ interview as he explained how finishing The Fall-Off changed his plans.
item.content:encoded:
J. Cole rejected retirement talk in a new GQ interview, saying his plans changed as he finished The Fall-Off.

He had intended the album to be his last. The rapper spoke with longtime mentor Mark Pitts and GQ’s Frazier Tharpe during Labor Day weekend in Las Vegas.

“No, I’m not using that word at all,” Cole said when Tharpe asked about retirement.

He described feeling drained during the album’s creation before finding fresh drive to make music. Pitts had doubted he was through.

“Luckily, by the time I got to actually finishing the album, because of the circumstances, it’s like, oh, nah, I’ll never say I’m going to retire. I don’t know whenever the next thing is going to happen, but, I’m definitely not going to say no,” J. Cole explained.

Cole had been thinking about retirement long before this interview.

In his 2021 SLAM cover story, when The Fall-Off was still in development, Cole explained that he wanted to push his skills far enough to feel satisfied if he never made another album. Finishing that work would also give him room to pursue other interests.

He traced the idea to the period after 2014 Forest Hills Drive and its tour. Success had let him slow down, but he soon questioned whether he had done all he could as a writer and producer. He told SLAM that he began working on The Fall-Off in early 2016 while making 4 Your Eyez Only.

Even then, Cole would not commit to a final album. He told SLAM he could not know whether he would want to record again several years later.

The work was meant to let him walk away with no regrets, while leaving room to return if he felt inspired. He also described daily writing as practice that had helped him build The Warm Up.

The finished album arrived February 6 as his seventh studio release. Its concert run gave that long project a much larger stage: the original announcement mapped out more than 50 cities in over 15 countries. The run was announced to start July 11 in Charlotte, North Carolina, at Spectrum Center.

As AllHipHop previously reported, “The Fall-Off Tour” was his first solo headlining trek since “The Off-Season Tour” in 2021. It also marked his first full global run since 2017’s “4 Your Eyez Only World Tour.”

The announced itinerary stretched through Europe, Australia and New Zealand before a December 12 finale at Johannesburg’s FNB Stadium.

For now, Cole told GQ that he wanted more time with family while touring and hoped to do more production.

item.title: G. Dep Performs At “Redemption Songs Live”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: G. Dep performed at New York's "Redemption Songs Live," where prison songwriters' music reached a crowd of more than 400.
item.content:encoded:
G. Dep took the stage at New York City’s Merkin Hall on Wednesday (October 28) for “Redemption Songs Live,” a concert centered on music written in prison. The Harlem rapper made a guest appearance before a crowd of more than 400, according to The Marshall Project.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani opened the night, which also featured musicians who had served time. Rapper Izzy Ali performed “State of Emergency,” which he wrote at Sing Sing. Alfred Roberts sang “Victory,” a song he wrote while in prison in New York.

The Kaufman Music Center program paired songs with news reports about the people who made them and the places where they were written. The Marshall Project and Musicambia, a group that teaches music in prisons, put on the event, which used songs, spoken stories, photographs and film. Blues, soul and rap were all part of the night. Its stories reached from the Jim Crow South to today’s ICE detention centers.

Reporter Maurice Chammah’s work helped shape the night and its look at how music has been made behind bars. The lineup brought him together with Lawrence Bartley, publisher of The Marshall Project Inside, and the Cambia Collective. The band is made up of Musicambia teachers and past students. The venue listed a 7 p.m. start at 129 West 67th Street.

For G. Dep, the appearance came more than two years after AllHipHop reported his release from Fishkill Correctional Facility in April 2024. Born Trevell Coleman, the former Bad Boy Records artist left prison on parole after spending more than a decade behind bars.

He had confessed in 2010 to a 1993 shooting that killed a man. New York Governor Kathy Hochul granted clemency in December 2023, before he was freed the next spring.

His time in custody also included college work: He earned an associate’s degree in liberal arts. At the time of his release, he planned to keep studying and pursue a bachelor’s degree in business.

Musicambia teaches people to play instruments and write their own music at Sing Sing Correctional Facility and other prisons across the country. The venue listed both Musicambia and The Marshall Project as groups that would share the concert’s proceeds.

item.title: MF DOOM Gets New Visual Treatment Thanks To Legend Sanford Greene
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: MF DOOM's estate enlisted Sanford Greene for an art collaboration that draws on the rapper's legacy and comics culture.
item.content:encoded:
MF DOOM’s estate enlisted comics artist Sanford Greene for its Collectionzz Artist Series, giving the masked MC’s legacy a new visual treatment.

The collaboration with Rhymesayers Entertainment will launch October 29 at 11 A.M. ET, according to the estate’s announcement.

“DOOM’s legacy keeps growing because he was ahead of his time. His music is timeless to me and so many others, which is why so many different communities continue to champion his work. I wanted to express that legacy through body language. In this image, he’s sitting like a king, absorbing his accolades and engulfed in adoration, looking back at the journey,” Sanford Greene said.

That approach gives the rapper’s villain persona room to reflect, with Greene focused on the man taking what he’s due.

Greene brings years of experience drawing Black characters to the project. His credits include Marvel’s Power Man and Iron Fist and cover art for Black Panther and Luke Cage. His work has also appeared at DC, Dark Horse and Image, crossing both major superhero publishers and creator-owned comics.

At Image, he created Bitter Root with David F. Walker and Chuck Brown. The series follows the Sangerye family, monster hunters facing supernatural threats in 1920s New York.

Its Harlem Renaissance setting places the fight amid a major era of Black art and culture. Family losses and disputes over how to fight evil shape the story alongside its monsters.

Greene has also brought Hip-Hop artists into the comics world.

He handled the artwork for Marvel and Mass Appeal’s Legend Has It… project, with Brandon Thomas writing.

That collaboration recast artists including Nas, Ghostface Killah, Raekwon and Slick Rick as comic characters. It tied the visual storytelling to Mass Appeal’s album series, giving Greene another direct link between rap’s larger-than-life figures and the way they appear on a comics page.

DOOM’s own history makes that connection easy to follow.

Before the mask, listeners knew him as Zev Love X in KMD. He appeared on 3rd Bass’ “The Gas Face” before KMD released its 1991 debut, Mr. Hood.

After his brother and fellow group member Subroc died, he later returned with the DOOM identity. Rhymesayers’ artist biography traces that return to 1997 and describes a producer who pulled from rap, R&B and cartoons.

The character and the sound grew together.

Artwork, items and prices will be revealed at launch. Orders are preorders, with shipping planned for the week of December 7.

item.title: Paris Jackson Seeks Estate Fee Cut As $100M Request Fuels Dispute
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Paris Jackson sought lower fees over Michael Jackson estate records as its managers rejected her claims and defended their pay.
item.content:encoded:
Paris Jackson asked a Los Angeles judge to cut the fees paid to the people running Michael Jackson’s estate, saying John Branca had failed to provide complete financial records.

Her request would lower the rate from 15% to 10% of gross entertainment-related income for 2023, 2024 and each year afterward until a complete 2026 accounting was filed, according to Deadline.

“Executor has violated the Court’s April 24, 2026 order by failing to meet his own self-selected, and then extended, deadline,” her motion alleged.

Her lawyers said the 2023 records were incomplete and the 2024 submission was a placeholder. They also challenged proposed compensation above $100 million, which covered both the co-executors and the law firm Ziffren.

The estate rejected the demand in its Wednesday response. Its representative said the executors had waived executor compensation from the start and had never collected it.

The representative described their pay as “a separate, court-ordered management fee for operating the hugely successful Michael Jackson business,” according to Billboard.

The estate also said it had filed the 2023 and 2024 accountings. Its response put the due dates for the 2025 and 2026 reports six months and 14 months away, respectively.

Paris had already won a fight over legal spending this year. Judge Mitchell Beckloff rejected $625,000 in bonuses for outside law firms in a May 13 ruling, ABC News reported. Branca and co-executor John McClain had authorized those payments for work in the second half of 2018. She had objected to those payments in June 2025 when the executors sought court approval for the lawyers’ bills.

Their attorneys told ABC News they disagreed with the ruling but would respect it. They stressed that the bonuses went to outside lawyers and that none of the $625,000 had been paid to the executors themselves.

The estate’s business decisions have also faced objections elsewhere in the family. In 2024, Katherine Jackson lost an appeal seeking to stop a deal to sell half of Michael Jackson’s catalog to Sony. The transaction was valued at roughly $600 million. The court upheld the executors’ authority to make the sale under his will.

A hearing on Paris’ fee dispute was set for December 4 before Judge Mitchell Beckloff.

item.title: Latto Sets First Africa Show In Lagos On Her Birthday
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Latto will celebrate her birthday at Flytime Fest in Lagos, with organizers billing it as her first performance in Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Latto will spend her birthday onstage in Lagos, where Flytime has booked her for what organizers call her first live performance in Africa.

The Atlanta rapper is set to play December 22, 2026, at the Eko Convention Center. Her show opens Flytime Fest Powered by Coca-Cola, which runs December 22-24. She is the first artist announced for that three-night festival. The dates fall during Lagos’s “Detty December” holiday season.

“Latto is a powerhouse performer, and her energy is a perfect fit for Flytime Fest,” Flytime Chief Operating Officer Keke Hammond told AllHipHop.

The Lagos date follows a fall spent touring with Doja Cat.

As AllHipHop previously reported, Latto joined the North American leg of the “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” as its special guest. The run began October 1 in Detroit and is scheduled to end December 1 at Madison Square Garden in New York.

That leaves three weeks between the tour’s planned close and her performance in Nigeria. The 31-date North American run also includes stops in Atlanta, Miami and Toronto, according to Pollstar’s tour report.

Her latest album already has a Nigerian connection. Wizkid joined Odeal on “Anxious,” a track from her fourth studio album, Big Mama.

Released May 29 through Streamcut and RCA Records, the project also includes “Okayyy” with Doja Cat. Teyana Taylor, Sexyy Red and 21 Savage are among its other guests.

Flytime’s wider December calendar starts two days before Latto’s set.

Brandy will headline House of R&B on December 20. Lil Baby, Kehlani and Yung Miami are booked for Coca-Cola Rhythm Unplugged on December 21. All those events are set for the same Lagos venue.

The company launched Rhythm Unplugged in 2004 and Flytime Fest in 2017. Past performers across its events include Megan Thee Stallion, Gunna, Wizkid and Burna Boy.

Flytime Circle closes the six-day calendar on Christmas Day. Organizers said they’ll announce more names for Flytime Fest and Flytime Circle in the coming weeks.

item.title: Carol Maraj & Audrey Jackson Bring Domestic Violence Talk To Canarsie
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Carol Maraj and Audrey Jackson discussed abuse, survival and personal boundaries at the first Café Conversations in Canarsie.
item.content:encoded:
Carol Maraj and Audrey Jackson brought a conversation about surviving domestic abuse to Canarsie, opening Café Conversations at Jackson’s Pop’s Place on October 23.

Nicki Minaj’s mother discussed her book, “Bruised But Not Broken,” with Pop Smoke’s mother at the restaurant and event space dedicated to the late rapper, according to BK Reader. Jackson chose the subject to launch the series during Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

“I wanted to bring conversations like these to the community,” Jackson said, explaining her wish to give people a place to talk openly.

The discussion covered boundaries. Jackson described learning that being welcoming did not require giving up her own limits.

The book connects Maraj’s own history with tools for readers. On her official website, Maraj describes a memoir that follows her life from Trinidad and Tobago to New York. It addresses both physical violence and the psychological harm of a controlling relationship.

The book’s description also lists material on isolation and manipulation, along with help recognizing warning signs. Chapters include Bible passages for reflection. A resource section explains forms of abuse and includes safety planning, while other sections address setting boundaries and regaining independence.

Maraj’s advocacy also extends to her foundation. Its website dates the organization to 2012 and lists domestic abuse education, counseling and workshops on peaceful ways to resolve conflict among its programs.

Jackson’s work in Canarsie has its own history. The Shoot For The Stars Foundation describes its mission as carrying forward Pop Smoke’s plans to help young people find opportunities, including those who felt poorly served by traditional schooling. Its account says he had approached educators about donating computers and other technology to local schools before his death in 2020.

That work has included Pop Smoke Day celebrations in Brooklyn. The Canarsie Courier reported that the July 20 birthday event brought a parade to Canarsie Park, with sports and performances. Alongside the sports, organizers offered yoga, activities for parents and children and a train ride. Vendors lined the route from the park entrance toward its basketball courts. Councilwoman Mercedes Narcisse presented Jackson with a City Council citation for her work serving the neighborhood.

item.title: Eminem Stalking Defendant Faces $250K Bond
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: A woman faced a stalking charge after allegedly violating an order to stay away from Eminem. Bond was $250,000.
item.content:encoded:
Eminem was the target of an alleged no-contact violation that led to a felony stalking charge against Nicole Gwen Savage.

The Trenton woman, 46, allegedly went to his Clinton Township property Tuesday, October 27.

His security called police, WDIV reported. Savage was arraigned Wednesday in 41B District Court on aggravated stalking, carrying up to five years.

Bond was $250,000 cash or surety, without a 10 percent option. Release requires GPS monitoring; she cannot contact Eminem, have weapons or leave Michigan. Authorities did not explain the earlier order.

A separate case involving Matthew David Hughes brought a prison sentence on June 17, 2025.

As AllHipHop previously reported, a jury convicted Hughes of aggravated stalking and first-degree home invasion after he entered the rapper’s property in August 2024.

His sentence requires at least 18 years in prison before he can seek parole.

That case had roots in an earlier break-in. In April 2020, Hughes used a brick to break a window and got inside while Eminem slept. Security stopped him and police arrested him.

A plea deal on a reduced second-degree home invasion charge followed in 2021. He received probation along with credit for the time he had already spent in custody.

Hughes later violated probation. During the 2024 intrusion, he got through a door that was unlocked, took a bicycle and ran after security spotted him. Police caught him at a Walmart four days later. Eminem testified at the May 2025 trial, which lasted two days.

The jury took less than half an hour to reach its verdict. The court also barred Hughes from contacting Eminem. In that case, prosecutors argued his conduct showed a dangerous fixation on the rapper.

For felony defendants in Michigan, a probable cause conference offers a chance to address what happens next.

The Michigan Judicial Institute’s checklist calls for the prosecutor, defendant and defense lawyer to discuss a possible plea deal. Bail is also on the agenda, including a chance to ask for a change in bond. Both sides can address agreements about facts or procedure and other issues they agree should be discussed.

Savage’s conference is set for November 9 at 8:30 a.m.
